prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Robins in the cottonwoods, holding still as the thin snow comes. The sun seems to flood them with blood. They have settled in the empty branches while the storm-lamps spit in your limbs, red evening swinging across the sky then dropping, ragged, into your frame to stay with you as you move and smile and have opinions. Then a woman’s torso white with dawn— their rich perch is yours, there is nothing you need to expect or retrieve, like warm fields floating toward an invisible moon. A person learns stone-throated composures and barters for days of calm weather, like a man in a dream who understands the answering pressure of eyes—you ask too much. But the birds are not reckless. Every minute their fat shapes are filling with sun, and I apprentice myself to their candor. Their bodies drift on the moving branches, solid— they are not taking and keeping. They are not torn papers in a rumor of wind, their small backs brown fields holding thunderclouds up. Inside their bodies, nothing falls to the earth and dies.

outputs.L2: Motionless among the bare cottonwood limbs, robins wait as fine snow drifts down. Sunlight seems to soak their feathers in crimson. They've taken residence in the stripped branches while tempest-lanterns crackle through your arms and legs—crimson twilight arcs overhead before falling, torn and uneven, into your body, remaining there as you walk through the world, grin, and voice your beliefs. Next comes a woman's chest, pale with morning light—that lavish perching spot belongs to you now; there's nothing left to anticipate or reclaim, much like sun-warmed meadows drifting toward a hidden moon. One learns to master a granite-voiced calm and negotiates for stretches of peaceful weather, resembling a dreaming man aware of eyes returning his gaze—you're demanding too much. Yet these birds show no carelessness. Each passing minute, their plump forms grow heavy with sunlight, and I make myself their student in honesty. Their bodies sway upon the shifting boughs, substantial and unwavering—they neither seize nor hoard. They aren't scraps of paper scattered by rumored wind; their small brown backs resemble fields that bear the weight of storm clouds without collapsing. Within their bodies, nothing ever plummets earthward to perish.
outputs.L3:
# The Red Hour

The robins have gone still in the cottonwood, three or four of them, maybe more, their small bodies arranged among the bare branches like something deliberate, like punctuation in a sentence the winter is writing. Snow falls thin and unhurried around them, each flake catching what light remains. The sun, low and dying beautifully as it always does, pours itself into their feathers until the birds seem soaked in red—not reflecting the light so much as absorbing it, becoming momentarily made of it.

I watch this from where I stand, and the same red light finds its way into me. It does not simply illuminate; it enters, settles somewhere beneath the sternum, and stays. I carry it with me afterward—through the small business of the evening, through whatever I say to whoever asks, through the shape my face makes when I mean to smile and does. The light does not announce itself in these moments. It simply persists, quiet cargo, coloring things from the inside.

I think about the birds and what separates us. We are the ones who learned early to arrange our faces, to compose ourselves into something presentable before we step out into the day. We negotiate constantly with existence—asking for good weather, good news, a good life, as though these things were owed to us, as though enough asking might tip the scales. We want too much and guard too carefully against too little. The robins do neither. They do not brace themselves against the cold, do not perform serenity or negotiate with the coming dark. They are simply present in their small solid bodies, unguarded because they have nothing to guard, unreckless because recklessness requires a self aware enough to endanger.

I find myself wanting to apprentice to this—to whatever it is that allows a bird to sit in a snow-heavy tree and simply be a bird, without ceremony, without complaint. Their bodies are compact and sure, weighted with a kind of certainty I cannot name. They do not take life in fistfuls, nor do they hoard it against future loss. They are not, as I so often feel myself to be, like torn paper caught in a rumor of wind—fluttering, insubstantial, blown by whatever forces happen to be passing through.

Something in their small forms holds together in a way mine does not. Nothing within them seems to slip loose or fall forgotten to the ground. Whatever they are, they are entirely—complete, sealed, whole in some manner I can only witness and not yet understand. I stand beneath the cottonwood as the light goes from red to violet to gone, watching them hold their stillness, wanting whatever wholeness lives inside their small red-lit bodies, wanting to learn, before the snow stops falling, how a thing survives by simply, entirely, being itself.
outputs.L4:
# Winter Robins

The cottonwoods hold their silence
in coats of early snow, branches
bent low with the weight of white,
and into this stillness they come—
a hundred robins, maybe more,
settling like punctuation marks
across the gray architecture of winter.

The sun goes down blood-red tonight,
bleeding through the bare lattice
of limbs, a storm-lamp swinging
low on the horizon's edge,
and still the robins do not stir
with any urgency, any need
to name what they are witnessing.

I have wanted so many things
in this life—the way the light falls,
the way a season turns its face
before I'm ready, the way desire
builds itself a house of ice
that melts before I've moved in.
But these birds ask nothing of the dusk.

They do not measure the sun's descent
against some private hourglass,
do not mourn the summer's green
persistence now fled south
or hoard against the coming cold
some memory of warmth. They simply are—
red-breasted commas in the falling dark,

perched on the thin architecture
of now, unburdened by before
or after. Their solidity
is not stubbornness but a kind
of candor, an honesty of being
that I have spent my whole life
circling, wanting, and never quite

landing in. The storm-lamp sun
sinks lower, and still they stay,
untroubled by the shifting light,
by winter's slow encroachment,
by anything at all, it seems,
except the branch beneath their feet,
the cold air moving through their feathers,

this single moment holding them
the way a hand holds water—
not gripping, only cupping,
letting what comes pass through
and what remains, remain.
I watch them until the dark
swallows the last red edge of sun,

and something in me settles too,
some restless argument goes quiet,
some grasping habit loosens
its long fingers from my chest.
Perhaps this is what peace looks like:
not resolution, but residence—
the willingness to perch, and stay.
outputs.L5:
# Robins: Nature's Cheerful Messengers

Robins are among the most beloved birds found in gardens and woodlands across many parts of the world. Known for their distinctive orange-red breast and melodious song, these small birds have captured the hearts of nature enthusiasts for generations.

The robin holds a special place in folklore and culture. In British tradition, the robin has become closely associated with winter and Christmas, often appearing on holiday cards and decorations. They are frequently seen as symbols of renewal, hope, and the changing seasons, as their arrival is often associated with the coming of spring in many regions.

They are remarkably adaptable creatures, thriving in diverse habitats ranging from forests and meadows to suburban gardens and parks. This adaptability has allowed robins to maintain healthy populations even as urban development has changed much of their natural habitat.

Behaviorally, robins are known for their territorial nature, particularly during breeding season. They will vigorously defend their chosen territory, often engaging in aggressive displays against rivals. Despite this territorial instinct, they have also developed a reputation for being relatively unafraid of humans, often approaching gardeners as they work the soil in hopes of finding disturbed insects and worms.

Robins typically build cup-shaped nests using grass, twigs, and mud, carefully positioning them in sheltered locations such as tree branches, shrubs, or even man-made structures like sheds and fence posts. The female usually lays several pale blue eggs, and both parents may take part in feeding the young once they hatch.

Their diet consists mainly of insects, worms, and berries, making them beneficial visitors to gardens as natural pest controllers. During colder months, they often shift their diet to include more fruits and berries when insects become scarce.

The robin's song is particularly noteworthy, as they are one of the few bird species that sing throughout much of the year, including during autumn and winter when many other birds fall silent. This persistent vocalization has contributed significantly to their popularity and recognition among casual birdwatchers and ornithologists alike.

Whether encountered hopping across a lawn in search of food or perched on a branch delivering their distinctive song, robins continue to bring joy and connection to nature for people of all ages.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem about robins in winter trees that blends nature imagery with fragmented human emotion and abstract philosophical musings.
counterfactuals.output:
# Robins in the Bone-White Hour

The trees have forgotten their names,
standing there like sentences
with all the verbs removed—

and still the robins come,
small punctuation marks
of impossible red,
stitching breath into the gray.

*What is a season but a grief
that learned to wear a coat?*

I watch them from the window,
my hands two strangers
folded in my lap, negotiating
the terms of stillness.

One robin, throat-full of some
older winter, tilts
its head at nothing—
or at the nothing
that is also me,
watching.

We are all just weather
wearing the wrong century.

The branch does not know
it is a branch. The cold
does not know it is unkind.
Only I know these things,
and knowing is a kind of frost
that settles in the chest,
white and particular.

*Somewhere, a self I used to be
is still standing in a doorway,
not yet decided
if it will snow.*

The birds don't ask
what any of this means.
They simply are the red
against the white against
the gray against
the long erasure
of the afternoon—

small hearts
beating like a question
no one asked,
answered anyway,
over and over,
in the leafless dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem in the style of James Wright or Robert Bly, using deep image techniques and startling metaphors about birds, snow, and the self.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Snow Knows About Flying**

I have been standing so long in this field that the crows have begun to nest in my collarbones. Snow falls the way forgetting falls—slow, then all at once, erasing the fence line, the barn, the small stubborn history of my footprints. Somewhere under all this white, a heartbeat is trying to remember whose chest it belongs to.

A single sparrow drops from the gray wafer of sky like a period at the end of a sentence God grew tired of writing. It lands on the black bones of an elm and becomes, for a moment, the only punctuation in the world. I envy it the simplicity of its hunger—one seed, one branch, no need to justify the shape of its small brown grief.

There is a self inside me that is only snow falling on water, disappearing the instant it arrives, and there is another self that is the water, dark and moving underneath, refusing to freeze though the whole sky leans down to press its cold mouth against the river's skin.

The geese go over in the evening, crying something in a language I almost had, once, before I learned to speak in sentences instead of wingbeats. I want to tell them: wait, I remember the shape of that migration, I remember before I was a man standing still in snow, when I was only the urge to fly south, urgent and unashamed.

Now the last light goes out of the elm like a match dropped in deep water. The crows in my collarbones settle in for the night. Somewhere, a fox is writing its red signature across the white page of the meadow, and I am trying to read what it says about hunger, about the long survival of small warm bodies in a cold that does not think about us at all.

I stand here longer than I should. The snow keeps erasing me, patient as a mother undressing a child for sleep, and I let it, because underneath all this disappearing there might be something small and feathered, waiting to remember how to rise.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of lyrical, dreamlike poetry that meditates on birds as symbols of calm acceptance versus human striving and desire.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Birds Know

The sparrow does not ask the sky
for larger wings or bluer distance—
she takes the branch that holds her weight,
sings the only song she owns,
and calls this enough.

We are not sparrows.

We are the ones who count the miles
between what is and what might be,
who measure mornings by their lack,
who touch the given world
and feel it slipping,
already grieving what we haven't lost.

*

Somewhere a heron stands so still
the water forgets to notice him—
one leg, one thought, one hour
folding into the next
like paper into paper,
no edges, no urgency,
just the patient architecture of *now*.

I have stood that still exactly never.
My mind arrives before my body does,
already planning the departure
from the very ground I'm standing on.

*

The birds do not dream of other lives.
This is either their poverty
or their entire fortune—

I can't decide,
and the deciding
is so much like being human
it aches:

this endless arithmetic of wanting,
this appetite that finds no ceiling,
this reaching toward the reach itself.

*

At dusk the starlings gather into weather,
a thousand small surrenders
becoming one dark, fluid will—
they do not vote, they do not doubt,
they simply *turn*,
as if the turning were the only verb
that ever mattered.

I want to turn like that.
I want to want without the wanting
eating its own tail.

I want to land somewhere
and call it home
without already dreaming of the leaving.

*

Perhaps the birds are not so different—
perhaps they too feel something
like our hunger,
small and urgent in the breast,

but they don't build a house of thought
around each feeling,
don't move in,
don't stay.

They feel the wind and become the wind's answer.
We feel the wind
and write, for years,
about the feeling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem featuring robins in cottonwood trees, mixing sensory detail with strange, associative leaps between nature and the body.
counterfactuals.output:
**Robins, Cottonwood, Marrow**

The cottonwood drops its snow in July—
white seed-fluff catching in throat-hollows,
in the soft webbing between fingers,
and I think: this is what the inside of a wrist looks like
when you press it to light.

Robin on the low branch,
breast like a fist that's been punching
something orange all winter.
                              *thruk-thruk*
                                        *tit-tit*
His eye is a bead of iodine.
He is auditioning for the role of *your grandmother's heart*
in the years before the surgery.

Down here: the trunk's bark
splits into knuckles, into the geography
of a hand that's held too many hammers.
I put my palm against it—
                    cool,
                              alive in that slow vegetable way,
sap moving like something remembered
rather than something felt.

*        *        *

Somewhere in me a robin is also nesting.
Rib-cage as branch-fork,
lungs gone soft and grey as cottonwood down.
Every breath: a small bird
shouldering its way into spring,
throat opening into that liquid whistle—
                    *cheer-up, cheerily, cheer-up*

I want to say the tree is teaching me something
about patience, about roots,
but really it's just standing there
being enormous and full of birds
while I stand here
being smaller, being fewer.

*        *        *

Evening comes down like cotton settling.
The robins go quiet, or maybe
they've become the quiet—
red breasts folding into shadow-breast,
into the dark meat of the tree
where I imagine a second heart,
slow-beating, wrapped in bark,
pumping something thick and green
up through the fingers of the branches,
out into the last light,
into the small hollow bones
of every bird about to sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemplative poem about learning stillness from birds, using surreal, almost mystical language and shifting perspectives between "you," "I," and third person.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Heron Taught

I.

You stand at the water's edge so long
the herons forget you are not reeds.
This is the first lesson: disappear
by becoming exactly what you are.

The heron does not perform its stillness.
It simply has not decided yet
to move. There is no waiting in it,
only the long gray patience of a held breath
that was never going to be released
on any schedule but the fish's.

II.

I have watched this happen to other people—
watched them become the riverbank,
watched the birds walk closer, closer,
mistaking them for shadow, for stone,
for something that has always been there
the way stones have always been there.

But when I try, my stillness has a clock in it.
I am aware of being still.
The awareness ruins everything—
a held note that keeps checking
if it's still being held.

III.

She said: watch how the crane folds its own name
into its neck, becomes a question mark
that isn't asking anything.
This is not patience. Patience implies
a future being waited for.
This is just the crane, entirely,
in the only moment that exists,
which is also, somehow, all of them.

IV.

You will not learn this from trying.
You will learn it the way water learns
the shape of whatever holds it—
not by force, but by forgetting
it was ever going to be a river,
was ever going to arrive
somewhere else, was ever
anything but this exact
silver stillness, now,
mirroring a sky
that also doesn't know
it's being mirrored.

V.

The birds do not know they are teaching.
This is the last lesson, and the hardest:
that mastery looks like unknowing,
that the heron's genius is precisely
its failure to consider itself a genius,
its failure to consider itself at all.

I sit at the river's edge and I am thinking
about not thinking, which is its own
small tragedy, its own gray bird
that will not let me forget it's there,
lifting off just as I begin
to disappear, its wings unfolding
like a sentence I keep almost finishing,
like stillness that keeps almost arriving,
like you, like me, like some third self
watching from the reeds
who was never taught to leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
